body.summary: 70% predicted chance of an ER visit or hospital stay in 2018 (average survivor 29%). Status alert: alert from 43%, watch from 29%. Main drivers: $44,900 total health spending in 2017 (median survivor about $6,700); 26 night(s) in hospital in 2017; Age 85 or older (top-coded).
body.riskWords: Higher than most: about 7 in 10 like them had one
body.forEllie: Hospital risk 70% next year (high; average 29%), mainly nights in hospital last year. Association, not cause.

evidence.text: Predicted chance of an ER visit or hospital stay in 2018: 70%. In the alert tier, 57% of past survivors had one.
$44,900 total health spending in 2017 (median survivor about $6,700) (raises risk)

recommendations.text: Add to the proactive outreach list: a nurse call in the next 2 weeks and a clear same-day contact route instead of the ER.
High care use last year: review what drove it and whether one team owns the plan.
Nights in hospital last year: confirm a discharge follow-up plan and who to call first.
Older age: a lower bar for proactive check-ins is reasonable.
If a symptom is getting worse, call your cancer care team first: they can often help the same day without an ER visit.

profile.dataSource: MEPS 2017 survey (real survivor, ID reassigned by organisers)

body.caveat: Association, not cause: these factors flag who may need help; changing one is not proven to prevent an ER visit. Risk is from survey answers only (clinical records did not improve it).

body.outcome: Any ER visit or hospital stay in 2018 (outcome_acute_care_2018)

data.predictorsFrom: 2017 MEPS only (2018 file used for the outcome column only)

body.validation: 10x repeated stratified 5-fold CV on the development set, one row per survivor; OOF predictions averaged over repeats; 2000-sample patient bootstrap for 95% CIs; paired bootstrap for differences.

finalModel.name: Random forest (300 trees, min leaf 10) with sigmoid calibration, on 16 features: 2017 care use (ER, hospital stays and nights, office, outpatient, home health, prescriptions, spending), age, physical and mental health scores, distress, depression screen, self-rated health, missed work days
finalModel.chosenBy: nested cross-validation of a 37-candidate model search (runs/autoresearch): it won 6 of 10 outer folds
finalModel.explanations: TreeSHAP per survivor, converted to calibrated log-odds (analysis/explain.py)
finalModel.previous: L2 logistic regression on 34 survey-domain features (the first submission)

modelSearch.note: Nested CV: the whole 37-candidate search re-run inside each of 10 outer folds, so the scored model never saw its test fold. This is the unbiased estimate of what the chosen model does on new survivors.
modelSearch.powerNote: With 466 survivors and 134 events an AUROC gain needs to be about +0.056 to clear a 95% CI; the held-out set (199, about 57 events) has an AUROC standard error of about 0.04.

firstEvent.definition: Survivors with no ER visit or hospital stay in 2017; outcome = first acute care in 2018
firstEvent.estimate: nested CV of the model search (runs/autoresearch/round-nested-oof.csv), not the post-selection 10x5 CV
firstEvent.why: Prior acute care explains most of the ranking on the full target (the 2017 repeat users are easy to find). Finding the first event is the harder, more useful job for prevention.

clinicalRecords.verdict: No meaningful gain: clinical detail (stage, comorbidities) adds nothing even inside Synthea; Synthea-derived scores give the MEPS model at most a tiny Brier gain (about -0.001) and no clear AUROC gain. But a Synthea model on shared variables alone ranks real survivors about as well as the final survey model (tie within CI)
clinicalRecords.detail: (1) Inside Synthea (660 synthetic patients, 4033 person-years), clinical-only features (stage, metastasis, comorbidities, opioids, kidney function) add no signal over shared variables: AUROC 0.671 -> 0.670, d -0.001 [-0.008, +0.007]; stage is missing in 86% of person-years. (2) A Synthea model on shared variables only, applied unchanged to real MEPS survivors, ranks them at AUROC 0.686 [0.634, 0.740] with O/E 1.02, vs the MEPS model's 0.713 out-of-fold (paired d -0.026 [-0.068, +0.013]): the shared-variable risk pattern learned from synthetic records transports about as well as a model fit on the survey itself. (3) Added to the MEPS model: clinical-burden score d AUROC +0.004 [-0.003, +0.012], d Brier -0.0012 [-0.0022, -0.0001]; Synthea prior d AUROC +0.004 [-0.002, +0.010], d Brier -0.0009 [-0.0018, -0.0000]; stratum features (3 definitions) d AUROC between -0.006 and -0.003. (Q3 adds each Synthea score as one feature to the MEPS L2 logistic on 34 domain features, our earlier model; its reference AUROC is 0.663 with a wider C grid.) Without a shared key every Synthea feature is a function of variables MEPS already has, so a gain means the simulation is a useful prior at n=466, not that real stage or comorbidity data would help these patients. The submission uses a MEPS-only model (the calibrated forest).

clinicalRecordsDetail.design:
Do the synthetic clinical records (Synthea) add anything beyond the MEPS survey?

Usage: .venv/bin/python -I analysis/synthea.py [data]     (expects data/meps and data/synthea; run train.py first)
Writes analysis/out/synthea.json.

There is no key between MEPS and Synthea, so no individual can be linked. Three pre-registered questions:
  Q1 (inside Synthea): do clinical-only features (stage, comorbidities, metastasis, opioids, kidney function)
     add AUROC over the features both sources share? Person-years, CV grouped by patient.
     Pass: paired dAUROC 95% CI above 0.
  Q2 (transport): a Synthea model trained on shared features only, applied unchanged to MEPS dev survivors.
     Pass: AUROC CI above 0.5. Also reports calibration (O/E) to show the population shift.
  Q3 (increment in MEPS): add Synthea-derived features to the MEPS model, same repeated CV as train.py,
     paired against MEPS-only. (a) transferred "clinical burden" score = E[clinical part of the Synthea logit |
     shared features]; (b) shrunken stratum features (acute rate, advanced-stage share, comorbidity burden)
     under three stratum definitions. Pass: dAUROC CI above 0 or dBrier CI below 0.
Only MEPS survivors with breast, colon, lung or prostate cancer are aligned to strata (Synthea has only those);
everyone else gets the overall Synthea mean plus an "unaligned" flag.

vsMepsModel.note: Paired bootstrap: Synthea shared-variable model (never saw MEPS) vs the final MEPS model (calibrated forest) OOF predictions, same 466 survivors.

clinicalRecordsDetail.notAligned: MEPS survivors with only skin, melanoma, uterine, cervical, bladder, lymphoma or other cancers (Synthea has none) get the overall Synthea mean and an 'unaligned' flag. Individual records were never matched: with no key, a person-level join on age/sex/race/cancer would be mostly noise.

caveats: Associations, not causes. Prior acute care and poor physical function dominate; they mark need, not levers.

Small data: 466 development survivors, 134 with the outcome. The ranking gain over the baseline (nested CV +0.04) is not statistically significant; the gain in probability quality (log loss, Brier) is.
Subgroups with n < 30 or < 10 events (Hispanic, NH Asian, NH other, uninsured, colon, lung) are too small to judge.
MEPS is a US national sample; the Synthea clinical records are synthetic and resemble South Florida. Nothing from Synthea is evidence about real patients.

display.note: Plain-language summary for apps. Show headline, keyNumbers and howSure; put limits next to any risk number.
display.headline: Flags who may need the ER or hospital next year. Of the people it puts on alert, about 57% did; the average is 29%.

keyNumbers.label: of alert-tier survivors had an ER visit or hospital stay
events caught by calling the top fifth

howSure: The risk numbers are well calibrated: when it says 30%, about 30% of those people had an ER visit or hospital stay.
It ranks people somewhat better than the organisers' baseline (AUROC 0.71 vs 0.67), but with 466 survivors that gap could be chance.
All numbers are scored on people the model never saw (nested cross-validation).
display.insight: Heavy care use last year (ER visits, hospital nights, many prescriptions and visits) is the strongest sign of acute care next year. It marks need; it is not something to change directly.
display.nextQuestion: Who will have a FIRST ER visit or hospital stay? Of 326 survivors with none in 2017, 70 had one in 2018; no model finds them much better than the baseline yet (AUROC 0.65 vs 0.63).
limits: Associations, not causes: the factors flag who may need help; changing one is not proven to prevent an ER visit.
Built from survey answers only. The synthetic clinical records (Synthea) did not improve it and share no patient key with the survey.
NH Black: the model ranks risk poorly (AUROC 0.48, n = 47); use clinical judgement
display.perSurvivor: Each survivor's panel has headline, summary, evidence[] (top drivers in plain words, kind = topic), recommendations[] (audience = care-team | coach | survivor) and caveat (always show it with the risk).
